name: Dextroamphetamine (Dexedrine, Zenzedi, Xelstrym)
summary: Stimulant medication for ADHD and narcolepsy. Increases dopamine and norepinephrine to improve focus and wakefulness, but carries high risks of abuse, weight loss, and heart side effects.
description: Dextroamphetamine is a central nervous system stimulant used mainly for ADHD and narcolepsy. It boosts dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain to improve attention, reduce impulsivity, and promote wakefulness. It comes as tablets, extended-release capsules, oral solution, and a transdermal patch (Xelstrym). Because it is a Schedule II controlled substance, it has a high risk of misuse, addiction, appetite and weight loss, and cardiovascular side effects. Extra caution is needed in children, especially those younger than 6 years, where extended-release forms can cause higher drug levels and significant weight loss.
patient_summary: Dextroamphetamine is a stimulant used for ADHD and narcolepsy. It can help you or your child focus better, sit still longer, and stay awake. It comes as pills, liquid, and a patch. It is a controlled substance with a real risk of misuse and addiction. Common side effects include decreased appetite, trouble sleeping, weight loss, and feeling jittery. In very young children, long-acting forms (extended-release) can cause more side effects and serious weight loss, so they are usually avoided. Your care team will monitor heart rate, blood pressure, growth, appetite, sleep, and mood while you are on this medication.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved as part of a comprehensive ADHD treatment plan that includes behavioral, educational, and social interventions. Particularly useful for improving attention, focus, and reducing hyperactivity and impulsivity.
Used to improve daytime wakefulness and reduce excessive daytime sleepiness. Not all formulations are approved for narcolepsy (transdermal patch excluded).
Occasionally used in children with obesity secondary to hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, under specialist supervision and with strict monitoring for cardiovascular and growth effects.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to amphetamine products or any component (including angioedema, anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome with patch)
Use during or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) therapy (including linezolid or IV methylene blue)
Symptomatic cardiovascular disease or structural cardiac abnormalities
History of drug abuse or dependence (strong caution; often a relative contraindication)
Motor tics or family history of Tourette syndrome (Canadian labeling)

efficacy_response.patient_text: Most children and adults who tolerate dextroamphetamine notice clearer focus, better ability to sit still, and less impulsivity once the dose is adjusted correctly. Overall effectiveness is similar to other stimulant medications used for ADHD.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally; transdermal system provides continuous drug delivery over the wear period.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Not precisely defined; clinically effective at low milligram doses.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral immediate-release: within 1 to 2 hours; extended-release: later peak; transdermal patch: several hours after application.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral immediate-release: about 3 hours; extended-release: about 8 hours; transdermal patch: about 6 to 9 hours after initial application.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral: about 12 hours in adults; transdermal: about 6.4 to 11.5 hours in children and adults.
pharmacokinetics.duration_ER: About 8 hours for extended-release capsules; 9 hours for the transdermal patch while worn.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine; excretion is pH-dependent and increases in more acidic urine.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Acidic foods, juices, or vitamin C can reduce serum levels and effectiveness; external heat can increase absorption from the patch.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine is a stimulant used mainly for ADHD and narcolepsy. It is usually one part of a broader treatment plan that includes behavioral and educational support.
items: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): Helps improve attention, reduce impulsivity, and decrease hyperactivity at school, work, and home.
Narcolepsy: Helps people stay awake during the day and reduces sudden sleep episodes.
Extended-release transdermal patch (Xelstrym): Approved for ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older.
Immediate-release tablets and solution (Dexedrine, Zenzedi, ProCentra): Approved for ADHD in children as young as 3 years, though most modern guidelines prefer age 6 and older.
off_label: Obesity related to hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction in children and adolescents, under specialist care.
Occasional use in other sleep-wake disorders when standard treatments are not effective, under specialist supervision.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: People respond differently, but these are common experiences reported with dextroamphetamine when the dose is adjusted correctly.

quotes: I can actually finish tasks instead of bouncing between five things.
Schoolwork that seemed impossible now feels manageable.
My mind is quieter and I can focus on one thing at a time.
I feel more awake during the day and less like I’m fighting to stay conscious.
I no longer nod off in meetings or in class.
My narcolepsy naps are shorter and less frequent.
Food just doesn’t sound appealing at lunchtime.
Falling asleep at night is harder on days I take it later.
I feel a bit more tense or wired when the dose is too high.
items.note: Decreased appetite, weight loss, and trouble sleeping are very common, especially when starting or increasing the dose.

items.category: When the Dose Is Too High
quotes: My heart feels like it’s pounding or racing sometimes.
I feel jittery and on edge instead of calmly focused.
I get irritable and more emotional as it wears off.
items.note: Too high a dose can cause jitteriness, anxiety, mood swings, or a harsh "crash" as the medicine wears off.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine starts working the same day you take it. You do not need to wait weeks to notice an effect, unlike antidepressants.
key_points: Oral immediate-release: Starts to work in about 1 to 2 hours. Effects last about 4 to 6 hours.
Oral extended-release capsules (Spansules): Typically last around 8 hours, often covering the school or work day.
Transdermal patch (Xelstrym): Applied 2 hours before you need it to work, then worn for up to 9 hours; total effect covers most of the day.
Onset and duration vary between people and may be affected by food, stomach acid, and skin temperature (for the patch).

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Stimulants like dextroamphetamine are among the most effective medications in all of psychiatry. When tolerated, many children and adults have noticeable improvements in focus, ability to sit still, task completion, and overall functioning. Benefits often appear within days and are directly tied to when the medication is active in the body.
sections.clinical_details: Dextroamphetamine has similar effectiveness to other first-line ADHD stimulants such as methylphenidate. Treatment guidelines recommend stimulants as a primary medication option for moderate to severe ADHD, along with behavioral and educational interventions. Response depends on the right diagnosis, careful dose titration, and ongoing monitoring of benefits versus side effects.

citation.title: Clinical use of stimulant medications for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Dextroamphetamine is a Schedule II stimulant with high risks of abuse, addiction, and weight loss, especially in young children.
sections.black_box: Stimulant medications including dextroamphetamine have a high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to addiction, overdose, and death. Misuse by snorting, injecting, or taking higher doses than prescribed greatly increases the risk of serious heart problems and sudden death.
other: Extended-release stimulants and young children: In July 2025, the FDA warned that children younger than 6 years taking extended-release amphetamine and methylphenidate products had higher blood levels and more side effects, including weight loss of at least 10%. Because of this, the labeling now recommends against extended-release stimulants in children under 6 and emphasizes close monitoring of weight and growth.

Heart risks: Stimulants can increase heart rate and blood pressure. Rarely, they have been linked to sudden death, stroke, or heart attack in people with underlying heart disease. A careful heart history and physical exam are recommended before starting.

Psychiatric risks: Stimulants can worsen or unmask conditions such as bipolar disorder or psychosis in vulnerable patients, causing hallucinations, paranoia, or mania. New or worsening aggression, irritability, or mood swings should be reported.
Growth and weight: Long-term use in children can slow growth and cause weight loss. Height, weight, and appetite must be monitored regularly.
Peripheral vasculopathy and Raynaud phenomenon: Stimulants can reduce blood flow to fingers and toes, causing color changes, numbness, or pain. Rarely, ulcers or tissue damage can occur.

Serotonin syndrome: When combined with certain antidepressants or other serotonergic drugs, there is a risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, sweating, tremor, rapid heart rate, fever), which can be life-threatening.
patient_counseling: Take exactly as prescribed. Never share your medication with anyone, and store it securely. It has high street value and is a target for misuse.
Tell your doctor if you or your child has any heart problems, fainting spells, chest pain, or a family history of sudden death.
Monitor your or your child’s appetite, weight, sleep, and mood. Report big changes, especially rapid weight loss or growth slowdown.

In children younger than 6 years, extended-release stimulants generally should not be used. If a young child loses significant weight or has other side effects, your clinician may stop the medication or switch to an immediate-release option.
If you notice new hallucinations, paranoia, extreme mood swings, or unusual aggression, contact your clinician right away and stop the medication until evaluated.
Do not abruptly stop high or long-term doses without medical guidance, as this can cause severe fatigue, low mood, and other withdrawal symptoms.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common side effects include decreased appetite, weight loss, trouble sleeping, and feeling jittery. Serious but less common problems involve the heart, mood, and blood flow to fingers and toes.
plain_language_list: Decreased appetite and weight loss, especially around lunchtime or when doses are higher.
Trouble falling asleep or staying asleep if taken too late in the day.
Increased heart rate and blood pressure.
Skin irritation or redness at the patch site (for the transdermal system).

common.incidence: Very common (around 10% to 30% or more, higher in younger children and at higher doses).
common.patient_note: Your child may eat less at lunch and lose weight, especially on long-acting forms. Focus calories at breakfast and dinner, and monitor weight closely. In children younger than 6 years on extended-release stimulants, weight loss of at least 10% has been reported, prompting new FDA warnings.

common.incidence: Common (often 5% to 15% or more depending on dose and timing).
common.patient_note: Trouble falling asleep is more likely if doses are taken late in the day. Moving doses earlier, lowering the dose, or switching formulations can help.

common.incidence: Common, especially during the first weeks.
common.patient_note: Headache or stomach discomfort often improves with time or dose adjustments. Taking with food in the morning can help some people.

common.incidence: Common, especially as the medication is wearing off.
common.patient_note: Some people feel more irritable or emotional when the dose is too high or when it wears off quickly. Let your clinician know if afternoon or evening "crashes" are a problem.

common.incidence: Very common (redness, itching, irritation in most patch users).
common.patient_note: Mild redness or itching at the patch site is common and often improves by rotating sites. Severe rash, blistering, or swelling needs medical attention and may require stopping the patch.

serious: Serious heart problems: chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or signs of stroke (sudden weakness, trouble speaking, facial droop). Call emergency services immediately.
New or worsening psychiatric symptoms: hallucinations, paranoia, mania, extreme aggression, or suicidal thoughts.
Peripheral vasculopathy and Raynaud phenomenon: fingers or toes turning white, blue, or red with pain, numbness, or ulcers.
Severe allergic reactions: swelling of face, lips, or tongue; difficulty breathing; rash or hives. For the patch, widespread rash or severe skin reaction can occur.
Significant weight loss or failure to grow in children, especially with extended-release formulations and in those younger than 6 years.
Rhabdomyolysis (rare): severe muscle pain, dark urine, fever, or confusion.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Dextroamphetamine interacts with many medications and substances. Some combinations can be dangerous or are strictly banned.

items.with: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, linezolid, IV methylene blue
items.risk: Severe, potentially life-threatening increase in blood pressure and serotonin syndrome.
items.action: Contraindicated. Do not use dextroamphetamine during or within 14 days of MAOIs.

items.with: Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, St. John’s wort, tryptophan)
items.risk: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, sweating, tremor, fever, confusion).
items.action: Use with caution. Start at low stimulant doses, monitor closely, and seek urgent care for signs of serotonin syndrome.

items.with: CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Increased dextroamphetamine levels and side effects (heart rate, blood pressure, anxiety, insomnia).
items.action: May need lower stimulant doses and closer monitoring.

items.with: Other stimulants (other amphetamine products, methylphenidate, modafinil/armodafinil, caffeine in high doses)
items.risk: Additive stimulation, higher heart rate and blood pressure, anxiety, insomnia.
items.action: Avoid combining two stimulant prescriptions unless specifically directed by a specialist. Limit energy drinks and high-dose caffeine.

items.with: Acidifying agents (vitamin C, acidic juices, some antacids that acidify urine)
items.risk: Lower blood levels of dextroamphetamine, reducing effectiveness.
items.action: Avoid large doses of vitamin C or highly acidic drinks around dosing. Tell your clinician if the medicine seems weaker on certain days.

items.risk: Higher blood levels and longer duration of dextroamphetamine, raising side effect risk.
items.action: Use cautiously and separate timing where possible. Monitor for jitteriness, insomnia, or heart symptoms.

items.risk: Stimulants may reduce the effectiveness of blood pressure drugs.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure closely and adjust doses as needed with your cardiologist or primary care clinician.

items.risk: Increased risk of misuse, addiction, heart strain, and dangerous behaviors.
items.action: Avoid nonmedical use of alcohol or recreational drugs while on dextroamphetamine, especially at higher doses or with heart risk factors.

sections.heading: Stopping or Taking Breaks Safely
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine does not cause life-threatening withdrawal like some other drugs, but stopping suddenly after long-term or high-dose use can cause uncomfortable symptoms and a sharp drop in functioning.
key_points: Short-term, low-dose use: Many patients can stop without a formal taper, but may feel more tired, unfocused, or low in mood for a few days.
Long-term or high-dose use: Stopping suddenly can cause severe fatigue, low mood, increased appetite, sleep changes, and a strong contrast in ADHD symptoms.
Typical approach: Clinicians often reduce the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks, especially if there are mood vulnerabilities or high doses.
Drug holidays: Some families and clinicians use "weekend" or "summer" breaks in children to help with appetite and growth; this should be planned with the prescriber, not done randomly.
Underlying condition: Stopping or reducing the stimulant does not cure ADHD or narcolepsy; symptoms usually return when the medication is out of the system.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing is highly individualized. Clinicians usually start low and go up slowly each week until benefits are seen or side effects become limiting.

adult.adhd_transdermal_initial: 9 mg/9 hours patch applied once daily, 2 hours before effect is needed and removed within 9 hours.
adult.adhd_transdermal_titration: Increase to 13.5 mg/9 hours or 18 mg/9 hours at weekly intervals based on response and tolerability.
adult.adhd_transdermal_max: 18 mg/9 hours patch applied once daily (only one patch per 24 hours).
adult.narcolepsy_ir_initial: 10 mg by mouth once daily (tablet or solution), usually in the morning.
adult.narcolepsy_ir_titration: Increase by 10 mg per day at weekly intervals as needed.
adult.narcolepsy_ir_usual: 5 to 60 mg per day divided into 2 or 3 doses, spaced 4 to 6 hours apart.
adult.narcolepsy_er_usual: 5 to 60 mg per day as a once-daily extended-release capsule or in 1 to 2 divided doses (spacing 6 to 8 hours apart).
adult.renal_adjustment_transdermal: GFR 15 to <30 mL/min/1.73 m²: max 13.5 mg/9 hours patch; GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m²: max 9 mg/9 hours patch.
adult.timing: First dose immediately after waking. Avoid doses in the late afternoon or evening to reduce insomnia.

pediatric.adhd_ir_3_to_5: Start 2.5 mg by mouth once daily in the morning. Increase by 2.5 mg per day each week as needed. Usual max 40 mg per day in 2 to 3 divided doses. Guidelines generally discourage routine use in children under 6.
pediatric.adhd_ir_6_to_16: Start 5 mg once or twice daily in the morning (first dose as soon as awake). Increase by 5 mg per day each week as needed. Usual daily dose 5 to 20 mg per day; max 40 mg per day in 2 to 3 divided doses (4 to 6 hours apart).
pediatric.adhd_er_capsules_6_to_16: Start 5 mg once daily in the morning. Increase by 5 mg per day at weekly intervals. Usual daily dose 5 to 20 mg per day; max 40 mg per day in 1 to 2 divided doses (6 to 8 hours apart). In some patients over 50 kg, doses up to 60 mg per day have been used with careful monitoring.
pediatric.adhd_transdermal_6_to_17: Start 4.5 mg/9 hours patch once daily, applied 2 hours before effect is needed and removed within 9 hours. Increase by 4.5 mg/9 hours at weekly intervals to a max of 18 mg/9 hours patch.
pediatric.adhd_transdermal_18_plus: Start 9 mg/9 hours patch once daily, then titrate up as in adults.
pediatric.narcolepsy: Dextroamphetamine may be used orally in children 6 years and older or adolescents under specialist supervision, starting at 5 to 10 mg daily and increasing weekly, up to a total of 60 mg per day divided into 1 to 3 doses.

sections.simple_explanation: Immediate-release forms act quickly and wear off in about 4 to 6 hours, so they are often taken 2 or 3 times per day. Extended-release capsules and the patch give a smoother effect across the day and are usually taken or applied once in the morning.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine requires extra caution during pregnancy, breastfeeding, early childhood, older age, and in patients with heart, kidney, or liver problems.
sections.pregnancy: Use during pregnancy has been associated with risks such as low birth weight, preterm birth, and possible withdrawal symptoms in the newborn. For pregnant patients with mild to moderate ADHD, nonmedication strategies are preferred. For those with more severe ADHD or narcolepsy, the decision to continue medication should be made using shared decision-making, aiming for the lowest effective dose and minimizing other risk factors.
sections.lactation: Dextroamphetamine passes into breast milk. Small studies found relative infant doses around 2% to 13.8% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose, with no short-term adverse effects reported in a few infants. Because long-term neurodevelopmental effects are unknown and stimulants can affect heart rate, blood pressure, and growth, many manufacturers do not recommend use while breastfeeding. If used, monitor the infant for irritability, poor sleep, poor feeding, or poor weight gain.
sections.pediatrics: Stimulants are widely used in school-aged children with ADHD, but dextroamphetamine is not recommended for routine use in children younger than 6 years. In July 2025, the FDA highlighted that extended-release stimulants in children under 6 led to higher blood levels and more side effects, including significant weight loss. Growth (height and weight), appetite, sleep, heart rate, and blood pressure must be checked regularly.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults may be more sensitive to increases in heart rate and blood pressure and to mood or sleep changes. Start at the lowest possible dose and titrate very slowly, with close cardiovascular monitoring. Consider nonstimulant or nonmedication strategies when possible.
sections.hepatic: No specific dose adjustment guidelines exist, but because dextroamphetamine is partly metabolized in the liver, use with caution in moderate to severe liver impairment and titrate slowly.
sections.renal: Oral forms do not have clear renal dosing guidelines, but reduced kidney function may slow elimination. The transdermal patch requires lower maximum doses in reduced kidney function. In advanced kidney disease, careful dose selection and monitoring are required.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Cardiovascular status: Check heart rate and blood pressure at baseline, after dose increases, and periodically thereafter.
Cardiac history: Screen for structural heart disease, fainting, chest pain, and family history of sudden death or serious arrhythmias.
Growth and weight: In children and adolescents, track height and weight at least every 3 to 6 months; pay special attention to extended-release formulations and children under 6.
Appetite and nutrition: Ask about meals skipped, appetite changes, and dietary intake; consider nutrition support if needed.
Sleep: Monitor for insomnia or early-morning waking, especially if doses are taken later in the day.
Behavior and mood: Watch for increased anxiety, irritability, aggression, mood swings, or new psychotic or manic symptoms.
Peripheral circulation: Look for color changes, pain, numbness, or sores on fingers and toes suggestive of Raynaud phenomenon or peripheral vasculopathy.

Substance use and misuse: Ask about cravings for higher doses, using without a prescription, taking more than prescribed, or diversion. Check prescription drug monitoring programs (PDMPs) when appropriate.
Adherence and function: Review school or work performance, organization, attention, and symptom ratings from parents, teachers, or the patient.
Skin (patch users): Monitor for persistent or severe skin reactions at the application site or elsewhere on the body.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine comes in several forms so clinicians can match onset, duration, and flexibility to the patient’s needs.
items: Immediate-release tablets (Zenzedi and generics): 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 7.5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg.
Immediate-release oral solution (ProCentra and generics): 5 mg/5 mL, useful for fine-tuning doses and for children who cannot swallow pills.
Extended-release capsules (Dexedrine Spansule and generics): 5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg, designed for once-daily or twice-daily dosing with longer coverage.
Transdermal patch (Xelstrym): 4.5 mg/9 hours, 9 mg/9 hours, 13.5 mg/9 hours, 18 mg/9 hours, applied once daily for up to 9 hours.
Canadian formulations: Similar extended-release capsules and tablets are available under Dexedrine and generic names.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine increases levels of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain. It promotes the release of these chemicals from nerve endings and partially blocks their reuptake. In ADHD, this helps strengthen the brain circuits that support focus, planning, and impulse control. In narcolepsy, it boosts wake-promoting pathways, reducing excessive daytime sleepiness.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Dextroamphetamine is a core stimulant option in ADHD and a long-standing treatment for narcolepsy. For ADHD, stimulant medications (including amphetamine and methylphenidate products) are typically first-line pharmacologic treatments for school-aged children, adolescents, and adults with moderate to severe symptoms, alongside behavioral interventions. Choice among stimulants depends on individual response, side effect profile, formulation preferences (pills versus patch), comorbidities, and misuse risk. In preschool-aged children, behavioral therapy is emphasized first, and medications are used cautiously. In narcolepsy, dextroamphetamine is one of several wake-promoting choices and is often considered when other medications are not effective, not tolerated, or not accessible.

seo.title: Dextroamphetamine (Dexedrine, Zenzedi, Xelstrym): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, and Safety
seo.description: Dextroamphetamine for ADHD and narcolepsy: how it works, dosing for kids and adults, side effects (insomnia, weight loss, heart risks), July 2025 FDA weight-loss warning for extended-release stimulants in young children, and monitoring guidance.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and aligned with current FDA prescribing information, major ADHD and narcolepsy treatment guidelines, and the July 2025 FDA safety communication on extended-release stimulants in young children.

faqs.a: Dextroamphetamine is mainly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy. In ADHD, it helps improve focus, reduce hyperactivity, and decrease impulsive behavior. In narcolepsy, it helps people stay awake and reduces excessive daytime sleepiness.

faqs.q: How long does dextroamphetamine take to work?
faqs.a: Immediate-release tablets and liquid usually start working within 1 to 2 hours and last about 4 to 6 hours. Extended-release capsules tend to last around 8 hours. The transdermal patch (Xelstrym) is applied 2 hours before you need it to work and is worn for up to 9 hours, providing coverage for most of the day.

faqs.q: What is the July 2025 extended-release stimulants safety update?
faqs.a: In July 2025, the FDA reviewed data on extended-release amphetamine and methylphenidate products in children younger than 6 years. They found higher drug levels in the blood and more side effects, including weight loss of at least 10%. As a result, the FDA required updated labeling stating that extended-release stimulants are not recommended in children under 6 and that clinicians should consider stopping or switching to alternative treatments, such as immediate-release stimulants, if young children experience significant weight loss or other adverse reactions.

faqs.q: Is dextroamphetamine safe for children under 6?
faqs.a: Some immediate-release forms are technically approved for children as young as 3. However, modern guidelines generally recommend behavioral therapy first in preschoolers, and are cautious about using stimulants in this age group. Extended-release stimulants, including dextroamphetamine products, are not recommended in children younger than 6 due to higher drug exposure and more side effects, especially significant weight loss. If used at all, it should be under specialist supervision with very careful monitoring.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of dextroamphetamine?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are decreased appetite, weight loss, trouble sleeping, headache, stomachache, feeling nervous or jittery, and increased heart rate or blood pressure. Patch users frequently have redness or irritation where the patch is applied. Many side effects can be managed by adjusting the dose, timing, or formulation.

Yes, stimulants can slow growth in some children. Long-term use has been linked to smaller increases in height and weight compared with children who are not on stimulants. This is why height and weight should be monitored regularly. If growth slows significantly, your clinician may adjust the dose, take breaks from the medication, or consider other treatment options.

Dextroamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance, the same level as many other potent stimulants. It has a high potential for abuse, dependence, and addiction, especially when misused (taking higher doses, snorting, injecting, or using without a prescription). When taken exactly as prescribed and monitored closely, many people can use it safely, but it is still important to watch for signs of misuse or loss of control.

faqs.q: What heart risks should I know about?
faqs.a: Dextroamphetamine can increase heart rate and blood pressure. Rarely, serious problems like heart attack, stroke, or sudden cardiac death have been reported, usually in people with underlying heart disease. Before starting, your clinician will ask about personal and family history of heart problems and may check blood pressure, heart rate, and sometimes an ECG. Report chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or heart palpitations right away.

faqs.q: How is the patch (Xelstrym) different from the pills or liquid?
faqs.a: The patch delivers dextroamphetamine through the skin over 9 hours. It is applied once each morning and removed later in the day. It can be helpful for people who cannot swallow pills or who need more stable levels throughout the day. It commonly causes local skin irritation and is more expensive than many oral generics. Like other extended-release stimulants, it should not be used in children under 6 years.

faqs.q: Can I drink coffee or energy drinks on dextroamphetamine?
faqs.a: Small amounts of caffeine are usually safe but can add to the stimulant effect. Large amounts of coffee or energy drinks can cause jitteriness, anxiety, heart racing, and trouble sleeping. Many people do best with limiting caffeine while on dextroamphetamine.

faqs.q: Is it okay to take dextroamphetamine only on school or work days?
faqs.a: Some patients and clinicians use "drug holidays" on weekends, holidays, or summers, especially for children where appetite and growth are concerns. This should always be discussed and planned with your prescriber. Stopping and restarting randomly without a plan can make it hard to judge effectiveness and side effects.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop dextroamphetamine suddenly?
faqs.a: Stopping suddenly after short-term, low-dose use may just make you feel tired, hungry, and more unfocused for a few days. After long-term or high-dose use, you may experience a "crash" with fatigue, low mood, increased appetite, and sleep changes. It is usually safer to taper doses gradually with your clinician’s guidance, especially if you have depression or other mood conditions.

faqs.q: How does dextroamphetamine compare to Adderall?
faqs.a: Adderall contains a mixture of amphetamine salts (including dextroamphetamine and levoamphetamine), whereas dextroamphetamine products contain only the dextro isomer. Some people feel that dextroamphetamine gives a cleaner or smoother focus, while others do better on mixed amphetamine salts. Effectiveness and side effects vary between individuals, so the best choice is the one that gives good symptom control with the fewest side effects for you.
